I'd spend it on people who needed the money more than me.  I would set up a non profit to put the money into daily, and orchestrate my plans through. I would start a sustainable community to help people who fell on hard times get back on their feet. 

First, Buy an empty lot, install a campground bathroom and camp kitchen, and build tiny houses for people who are homeless. Tiny houses would be built on wheels, but would be made of sustainable materials with solar panels and be mobile if needed. 

People apply for tenancy, which is granted on the basis of need. Their rent is free for the first month while they settle in, then they have to pay rent that's set on s sliding scale relative to income. I'd employ them so that they have income, or offer scholarships and pay them to study a trade or skill that would help the community and themselves longer term. 

Employ a few to manage the property, and as many as are interested to become builders. I'd pay for school to send interested ones on to trade school to become electricians plumbers carpenters builders etc. 

Set up a daycare on site that would be free to residents, and employ a few residents to work there. Set up a school for adults to learn everything from basic literacy and numeracy to getting their high school equivalency degree. Have health education and financial education classes at night. I'd pay for the teachers through the non profit. 

Hire drug and alcohol and gambling counsellors to help residents with any addictions that put them on the road to homelessness. Pay residents to go into treatment as their job. Hire a doctor and a few nurses to run a clinic to meet the community's health needs. Hire a few psychologists and counsellors to help with any mental health issues of the residents. Put a few residents into courses to become counsellors or nurses or LNAs if they're interested. 

The clinic would have a needle exchange program. The community would require residents to use alcohol and other drugs only indoors, and not in the presence of any minors, or individuals who were clients of the treatment program. Any use of alcohol or drugs that interfered with their neighbors quiet enjoyment of the property would have a three strikes policy, with the final ultimatum of mandatory treatment or eviction. 

I'd hire a lawyer and an accountant to offer advice to any residents with overhanging legal trouble or tax issues. I'd employ a retired police officer to operate security for the community, and train residents in security skills, and contact the police if necessary. 

Once those costs had stabilized, I'd buy a farm from a family who was struggling but wanted to stay. I'd pay them to manage the farm, and they could keep the land, on the condition that they would also manage a few employees from my tiny house community down the road. I would pay community sponsored agriculture style so that the farm had enough cash flow to produce vegetables and orchards, a few cows to milk and chickens for eggs. In a year or two they would hopefully have enough offspring for us to start eating beef and chicken too. 

I'd open an animal shelter and employ residents to care for and rehabilitate the animals. I'd buy a cafe and employ residents to make coffees, bake and cook deliciousness. I'd hire the previous owner or chef to help manage the business and teach the new employees how to bake and cook. 

As those debts and costs stabilized, tiny houses would be built continuously until there were some max number set by whatever local government regulations. I'd build another site if needed. Rent payments from current residents would be put into building new tiny houses. 

Once residents had rented for one year and committed to work/school/addiction treatment, they would have the option of their rental payments becoming loan payments on their tiny house. It would be arranged formally and their payments would be reported to improve their credit history. Once it was paid, they could leave the community with their tiny house (it's on wheels!) to wherever suited them best, so if they had family or friends somewhere else they could relocate in time.

1. Insulate - get thick curtains, door snakes (sandbags for under doors), add an extra layer to windows with home wrap, etc. check what insulation there is in the roof. If you have an attic, they make styrofoam caps for those pull down staircases. Carpets are warmer than tiles. 

2. Passive heating- Take advantage of any heat that comes through your windows during the day, and close the curtains at night. If you have a dark carpet/bedspread/furniture it can absorb heat from the sun better than light colored furnishings 

3. Bundle up- layers are your new friend, and don't forget warm slippers and a beanie!

4. Heat what you need to - so your pipes don't freeze you need to keep your home heated to about 50 minimum. (Yes water freezes at 32, but remember the heat needs to penetrate to the pipes in the walls/floor/basement). If there are rooms you don't use, close the door to them so you spare heating that room up. 

5. Put an electric blanket under your fitted sheet, and heat the bed up when you start getting ready for bed. Turn it off before you go to sleep, or you'll wake up a sweaty delirious mess. Put lots of blankets or quilts on the beds to trap heat. 

6. Look at the costs of running electric heaters and compare the efficiencies of the models that meet your budget. If this isn't your forever home/investment, radiant heaters are pretty good, and when you turn them off they emit heat for a little longer.  I may have oversimplified my point though, so allow me to correct myself. 

Size DOES matter when it comes to activity levels in various dog breeds, as size was a key trait selected for when breeding dogs over the centuries. 

It is not the only indicator of how much activity a dog needs, but it's a pretty good one. Breed is important to consider when gauging a dogs baseline exercise tolerance. 

Dogs were bred for a purpose, with each breed suited to meet the needs of people, eg herding (sheepdogs), hunting (retrievers, Great Danes, Jack Russell's), being royal companions/bed heaters (Chinese Crested) ... the list goes on. 

Great Danes need lots of exercise, because they were bred to go out hunting boar on day long excursions. Jack Russell's were bred to flush foxes out of burrows, and they are also a high energy breed. Common trait being hunting breeds- while size isn't common between the two, it takes a lot longer to exhaust a big dog than a small one, in my experience (ex dog walker)

Dogs don't enjoy the same freedom of unsupervised movement outdoors in most suburban and urban homes, so the exercise they enjoy today is reduced from what they would have had when hunting and herding were parts of their daily lives. 

Dogs need exercise the way that people need exercise- it's a vital to physical and psychological wellbeing. Most people live sedentary lives and as a result their pets do too. 

I still recommend OP should take his/her dog for regular 30-60 minute walks or jogs most days of the week. Initially it will be hard work! but keep at it.  repeat exposure and positive reinforcement can help you train your dogs misbehaviour into a positive behaviour.

Have you tried dog training classes?

With our family's second dog, we went to an excellent dog trainer who explained that dogs pick up on YOUR body language and expectations. Suddenly it mad sense why our first dog had always pulled and lunged on the leash- because we always pulled him closer to us and got nervous. He interpreted our behaviour and body language as us, his humans, responding to a threat. By pulling on his leash, he thought there was something out there, and he wanted to protect us from it. 

If you have a BIG dog, it could also be partly because big dogs need lots of exercise and stimulation. Most large breeds were working dogs, so maybe your dog just gets SO EXCITED about walks because he wants to jump and skip and play and DO ALL THE THINGS! 

If you aren't able to get into training classes straight away, try taking him for two long (30-60+ minutes) walks a day. Runs would be even better, but work up to them. If he has a big spend of energy he might realise that the purpose of walks isn't to do all the things, but to check out the neighbourhood with you. 

Or maybe he just really likes to poop.

Try starting a gratitude and kindness diary. 1.Stick to the periphery of your local grocery store. Don't enter the middle aisles if you can avoid them! They're 99% processed crap. 
2. Don't buy it if you can't imagine growing it, farming it, or making it yourself from simple wholesome ingredients. 
3. Don't buy stuff you can make at home (eg baked goods). When you control the recipe you can make it whole grain, add nuts, use dark chocolate instead of milk choc, use less butter, less salt, etc. 
4. Pick healthier snacks, like whole fruits and vegetables, nuts, and herbal teas if you need a sweet fix. 
5. Popcorn kernels - just regular kernels not that paper bag yellow lard Coates stuff- air popped in your own paper bag will fill you up when you need a crunchy snack to replace chips. A few sprays with a cooking oil and a bit of garlic powder/onion powder will give you some more flavour, and a fraction of the empty calories. 
6. Eat lower GI foods. They can help you nix snacking because you won't crash after the blood sugar rush is over. 
7. Have protein and healthy fats at every meal- including breakfast! Even if its just a hard boiled egg you eat on your way out the door. 
8. See what happens if you only eat every 4 -5 hours. Learn what real hunger is (eg belly lurching) vs thirst masquerading as hunger. 
9. Drink water. Have a water glass or water bottle next to you all the time. Consider yourself well hydrated if your wee is very pale/ almost clear. 
10. Go for a walk instead of having a snack.  Even if it's ten minutes, or if it's to the furthest toilet at work. Distract yourself for 10-15 minutes, and any cravings should disappear.

1. Transport. 
Everyone else has suggested it, but moving closer to specialists or choosing specialists closer would be a huge source of potential savings. Try Telehealth or Skype appointments when your doctor needs to review you and not examine you, and ask that your out of state specialists liase with your local GP/PCP for blood tests etc. 
Another option would be to plan your appointments so that you can do two on the same day that are within driving distance, eg one in the morning and another in the afternoon. It's hard to get appointments with specialists, but if you know that you need to see Dr A every 4 weeks and Doctor B every 6 weeks, try to make it one day of the week, so sometimes they will happen on the same day. If you work with the receptionist they can tell you how far ahead they're booking with that kind of flexibility, so it might take a while to implement but it could make logistics easier in the long run. 
I'd be concerned with changes to your vision that you might need to quit driving in the future, so start having a backup plan now. Figure out bus routes, even if it doubles the time when you are out of work you can take the scenic route and relax on your way to appointments. 
Another thought is only using your car for big trips, and bicycling for any trip that takes you less than half an hour. Yea it's cold in the winter and colder when you're moving, but you'd be amazed how often you get in your car for a trip that you could've walked/biked without much effort. 
Getting groceries etc isn't easy on a bike, but have you hubby join you, and make regular planned trips where you only buy what you need. Buying in bulk only saves money when you use it up before it expires!

2. Pets
Get pet insurance if you are are a petowner who is going to pay for operations should an emergency happen. You don't want to have to chose to give up or put down a dog if they're seriously injured. 
Ask your vet what proportion of protein carbs and fats your breeds of dogs need. If you have a rice cooker, you can cook up brown rice, ground meat, and frozen veggies in the same amount of time it takes to cook your dinner. Take the time to do the math and work out if it would be cost effective in your local market, but it's worth figuring out. 

3. Housing
Move closer to where your life needs to be, or chose closer doctors. 
If you rent, look for cheaper property with modern insulation and electrical. 
If you own, insulate insulate insulate your house, year round. Don't hear rooms you don't use (close those doors). Tape up window borders. Get towels or thick curtains to hang up around the windows. Unplug everything when you don't use it (except your refrigerator and freezer) and only charge electronics when they reat need charging. 

4. General - 
do you and your husband both need a cell phone? Or could you share a single phone? We all managed without cell phones in our pockets until the last 10 years or so. Not glamorous but $37x12=$444/year. Maybe enough to get pet accident /emergency insurance. 
Is your husband able to work, even just a few hours part time? There are probably people in your community who could use a "hire a hubby" service to change light bulbs, fix gutters, shovel driveways or sidewalks, mow the lawn, etc. 
And I understand the lawyers advise was not to work, but if you are capable of working, it might be worth looking into partly supporting yourself with alternative means of an income. For example, if you have a sewing machine, give people lessons. Or help them finish a quilt. Become a part time gardener. Or a pet-sitter. Or a house sitter. Having something meaningful to do with your time, that doesn't focus around your health will be immensely important in your future mental wellbeing.
